rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The mutawatir nominal ḥusn replaces verbal-noun iḥsān, describing goodness as a quality rather than the act of doing good.
rows.anchor: Nominal form ḥusn instead of verbal noun iḥsān; shifts from

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The mutawatir karh reading, with fatḥa, suggests voluntary reluctance or aversion, unlike kurh's involuntary hardship.
rows.anchor: karh = voluntary reluctance/aversion vs. kurh = involuntary hardship

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If the second occurrence also has fatḥa (karh), both occurrences frame the mother's ordeal as reluctant rather than involuntary.
rows.anchor: Same vowel variant as word 9 — fatḥa on kāf; if both occurrences shift to karh

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The mutawatir faṣl is a shorter Form I verbal noun in place of fiṣāl, with the same meaning of separation or weaning.
rows.anchor: faṣl (verbal noun of Form I) instead of fiṣāl; shorter form, same meaning

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A canonical mutawatir variant puts kasra on the sīn of ʿasītum instead of fatḥa; both readings are forms of ʿasā with an attached pronoun.
rows.anchor: Vowel variant: kasra on sīn instead of fatḥa — both are canonical readings of ʿasā in the perfect with attached pronoun

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The mutawatir passive Form II reading means that the addressees were granted authority or made rulers, resolving the ambiguity toward governance.
rows.anchor: you were given authority, you were made rulers

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The mutawatir Form I reading means simple cutting rather than Form II's intensive fragmentation, reducing emphasis on repetition or thoroughness.
rows.anchor: Form I instead of Form II: simple cutting rather than intensive fragmentation

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The mutawatir sīn-for-ṣād substitution is dialectal and leaves the meaning unchanged while softening the pronunciation.
rows.anchor: Sīn replaces ṣād — dialectal ibdāl; semantically identical but phonetically softer

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In the mutawatir ishmām reading, ṣād carries a hint of zāy, an intermediate pronunciation between ṣ and s.
rows.anchor: Ishmām: ṣād pronounced with hint of zāy — intermediate phonetic realization between ṣ and s

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This mutawatir reading drops the hamza of raʾā for phonological ease; grammar and meaning remain unchanged, and it occurs in multiple canonical transmissions.
rows.anchor: Hamza of raʾā dropped entirely — phonological facilitation (tashīl); grammatically identical

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This mutawatir reading realizes hamza as a transitional glottal sound, between full hamza and its complete omission, reflecting dialect variation.
rows.anchor: Hamza realized as transitional glottal — intermediate between full hamza and complete drop

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The mutawatir madd reading lengthens hamza into ā, marking the interrogative with emphatic extension and rhetorical weight.
rows.anchor: Hamza prolonged into long ā vowel (madd) — emphatic stretching of the interrogative moment

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The mutawatir second-person plural reading directly accuses the addressees of following conjecture, instead of speaking about them in the third person.
rows.anchor: 2nd person plural (you follow) instead of 3rd person (they follow)

rows.speaker: Ibn Kathīr and others
rows.claim: Ibn Kathīr and others omit hamza in Qurān; the reading leaves meaning unchanged, smooths pronunciation, and reflects a Hijazi tendency to soften hamza.
rows.anchor: Hamza dropped: Qurʾān → Qurān. Ibn Kathīr and others read without hamza

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The nominative dhū makes it an adjective of ism rather than rabb, construing the name itself as possessing majesty and honor instead of describing the Lord.
rows.anchor: Nominative reading (dhū instead of genitive dhī) — makes dhū an adjective of ism

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The mutawatir Form V tafawwut shifts from reciprocal divergence in Form VI to intensive or reflexive fragmentation.
rows.anchor: Form V (tafaʿʿul) instead of Form VI (tafāʿul) — shifts from reciprocal divergence to intensive/reflexive fragmentation

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The canonical reading replaces the next verse's initial hamza in a-amintum with wāw, joining wa-āmintum across the verse boundary to nushūr.
rows.anchor: Canonical variant: hamza of a-amintum (next ayah 67:16) is replaced by wāw — wa-āmintum instead of a-amintum.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This canonical ishmām gives ṣād a slight zāy sound, preserving a trace of the word's non-Arabic origin as an intermediate pronunciation between sīn and ṣād.
rows.anchor: Canonical variant: ṣād with ishmām (slight admixture of zāy sound) — preserves a phonological trace of the word's non-Arabic origin

rows.speaker: Qālūn ʿan Nāfiʿ
rows.claim: The canonical sīn reading is closer to the etymological source Latin strāta and is accepted by Qālūn ʿan Nāfiʿ; it makes no semantic change.
rows.anchor: Canonical variant with sīn instead of ṣād — closer to etymological source (Latin strāta); accepted by Qālūn ʿan Nāfiʿ

rows.speaker: Nāfiʿ and Ibn ʿĀmir
rows.claim: Nāfiʿ and Ibn ʿĀmir omit hamza in saʾala, producing sāla and homophony with the verb meaning to flow.
rows.anchor: Hamza-drop: saʾala → sāla; Nāfiʿ and Ibn ʿĀmir reading removes hamza

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The masculine imperfect yaʿruju may agree with malāʾika as a broken plural or foreground rūḥ as the primary subject.
rows.anchor: Masculine imperfect — shifts grammatical gender of the verb, either treating malāʾika as a broken plural taking masculine agreement, or foregrounding rūḥ as primary subject

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The nominative rabbu permits either a fresh nominative restart or an independent predicate instead of genitive apposition.
rows.anchor: Case elevation reads rabbu, allowing a nominative restart or independent predicate rather than genitive apposition

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The nominative ar-raḥmānu can function as a nominative predicate or begin a fresh clause.
rows.anchor: Case elevation reads ar-raḥmānu, allowing the divine name to stand as a nominative predicate or fresh clause

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The nominative yawmu shifts from a temporal accusative to a nominative day/topic relation, allowing a more independent clause connection.
rows.anchor: Canonical nominative reading changes the case from temporal accusative to a nominative day/topic relation, allowing a more independent clause link.
